transitivity: both — transitive (end the meeting), intransitive (the movie ends late)
gloss: To stop, or to bring something to its finish.
examples: Let us *end* the meeting on time for once.
The concert *ended* just after eleven.
The strike has *ended* after nine long weeks.

transitivity: both — transitive (commence an investigation), intransitive (the trial commences Monday)
gloss: To begin, especially something formal or official.
examples: Boarding will *commence* in ten minutes.
The trial *commenced* on a rainy Tuesday in March.
Work on the bridge is *commencing* next spring.
contrast: *Commence* is the formal word — a schedule or a court uses it. In ordinary speech Americans say *start* or *begin*.

gloss: To be the one who starts a process or a course of action.
examples: Either side may *initiate* talks at any time.
The bank *initiated* a review of every account.
Who *initiated* the contact is still not clear.

gloss: To start a rule, a system, or an official process.
examples: The city plans to *institute* a curfew downtown.
They *instituted* a hiring freeze in January.
A new grading policy has been *instituted* for all first-year classes.

ru: возникать, брать начало; создавать, впервые ввести
transitivity: both — transitive (originate a style), intransitive (the custom originated in Spain)
gloss: To begin somewhere, or to be the first to create something.
examples: Most of our coffee *originates* in Colombia.
The tradition *originated* with a single family.
The phrase seems to have *originated* on the radio in the 1940s.
contrast: Intransitively it takes *in* or *from* for a place and *with* for a person: *originated in Spain*, *originated with her grandfather*.

gloss: To start something bad, usually by stirring other people up.
examples: Nobody could say who *instigated* the fight.
He likes to *instigate* an argument and then walk away.
The riot was *instigated* by a handful of outsiders.

gloss: To make something start happening, often suddenly.
examples: Cold air can *trigger* an asthma attack.
The announcement *triggered* a sell-off on Wall Street.
Opening the door without the code *triggers* the alarm.
contrast: The r is not doubled, because the stress is on the first syllable: *triggered*, *triggering* — compare *prefer → preferred*.

gloss: To set something off, especially a reaction or a conflict.
examples: One careless remark can *spark* a whole argument.
The video *sparked* protests in a dozen cities.
Her book has *sparked* a new interest in the subject.

transitivity: both — transitive (ignite the fuel), intransitive (the gas ignited)
gloss: To catch fire or set on fire, or to start something intense.
examples: A single spark can *ignite* the dry grass.
The comment *ignited* a week of angry replies.
Fuel vapor had *ignited* somewhere near the engine.

transitivity: both — transitive (kindle a fire), intransitive (the damp wood would not kindle)
gloss: To start a fire burning, or to start a feeling in someone.
examples: We used birch bark to *kindle* the fire.
That summer *kindled* his interest in birds.
The wet logs were not *kindling* at all.

gloss: To be the first to develop or use a method or idea.
examples: A small lab in Boston helped *pioneer* the technique.
She *pioneered* online teaching long before anyone else tried it.
The surgery was *pioneered* here in the 1970s.

gloss: To lead an effort or a campaign from the front.
examples: Two teachers will *spearhead* the fundraising drive.
She *spearheaded* the cleanup after the flood.
The project is being *spearheaded* by the youngest person on staff.

gloss: To make a serious event happen sooner than it would have.
examples: A bad harvest could *precipitate* a food crisis.
His resignation *precipitated* a week of chaos.
The war was *precipitated* by an incident at the border.

gloss: To start talking about a difficult or delicate subject.
examples: I am not sure how to *broach* the subject of money.
She finally *broached* it over dinner.
Nobody had *broached* the question of who would pay.
contrast: *Broach* sounds exactly like *brooch* (a pin you wear), but only *broach* is a verb. It also takes -es in the third person: *broaches*.

gloss: To be a sign that something important is beginning.
examples: Those clouds usually *herald* a change in the weather.
The invention *heralded* a whole new industry.
The deal was *heralded* as the start of a new era.

gloss: To begin, said of a day or a new period of time.
examples: The day *dawned* clear and bitterly cold.
A new era was *dawning* in American music.
When Monday *dawns*, all of this will still be here.
contrast: With *on* it means something different — to become clear to someone: *It finally dawned on me that she was joking.*

gloss: To formally order and pay for a piece of work to be started.
examples: The city wants to *commission* a mural for the wall.
They *commissioned* a study on traffic downtown.
The portrait was *commissioned* by her children.

gloss: To schedule something to start or happen at a set time.
examples: They will *slate* the hearing for early June.
The store *slated* its opening for the first of the month.
Construction is *slated* to begin in the fall.
contrast: In American English you meet it mostly in the passive: *is slated for Friday*, *is slated to begin*.

gloss: To formally admit someone into an organization or an honor.
examples: They *induct* five new members every spring.
He was *inducted* into the Hall of Fame last night.
The school is *inducting* its first class of honors students.
contrast: The preposition is *into*: *inducted into the Hall of Fame*.

gloss: To start dealing with a difficult job or problem.
examples: Let us *tackle* the garage this weekend.
She *tackled* the hardest chapter first.
We have been *tackling* the backlog one box at a time.

gloss: To start something again after it has stopped or failed.
examples: They plan to *relaunch* the app in the fall.
The magazine *relaunched* with a new editor.
The brand is being *relaunched* under a different name.

gloss: To make something work or apply again after it was turned off.
examples: You can *reactivate* the account within thirty days.
They *reactivated* her badge on Monday morning.
The old line is being *reactivated* for freight.

transitivity: both — transitive (reopen the case), intransitive (the road reopens Friday)
gloss: To open again, or to start considering something again.
examples: The bridge will *reopen* after the inspection.
Police *reopened* the case in 2019.
The museum has *reopened* with longer hours.

transitivity: both — transitive (reconvene the committee), intransitive (the group reconvenes at two)
gloss: To meet again after a break.
examples: We will *reconvene* after lunch.
The jury *reconvened* at nine the next morning.
The board is *reconvening* to vote on the budget.

gloss: To put a person, rule, or service back in place after it was removed.
examples: The union asked the company to *reinstate* the two drivers.
The city *reinstated* the late-night bus in October.
He was *reinstated* with full back pay.

gloss: To bring back something that had been dead or forgotten.
examples: Every few years somebody tries to *resurrect* the idea.
They *resurrected* a recipe from her grandmother's notebook.
The show has been *resurrected* for a tenth season.

gloss: To go back to an earlier state or an earlier way of doing something.
examples: If you do nothing, the settings *revert* to the defaults.
After a month the team *reverted* to the old schedule.
The land has *reverted* to forest.
contrast: It needs *to*: *revert to the old version*, never *revert the old version*.

ru: перегруппировываться, собраться с силами, взять паузу
gloss: To stop, get organized again, and then continue.
examples: Let us *regroup* after lunch and try again.
The team *regrouped* at halftime and won by six.
They are *regrouping* after a rough quarter.

gloss: To happen right after something else, as a result of it.
examples: A long silence *ensued*.
If the power fails, chaos usually *ensues*.
In the *ensuing* weeks nobody mentioned it again.

transitivity: both — transitive (terminate the contract), intransitive (the route terminates downtown)
gloss: To end something formally, especially a contract or a job.
examples: Either party may *terminate* the lease with sixty days notice.
They *terminated* the contract in June.
His employment was *terminated* without explanation.

gloss: To stop making, selling, or providing something permanently.
examples: The company may *discontinue* the smaller size.
They *discontinued* that model two years ago.
My favorite shade of paint has been *discontinued*.

transitivity: both — transitive (abort the launch), intransitive (the program aborted)
gloss: To stop something in the middle, before it is finished.
examples: The pilot had to *abort* the landing.
They *aborted* the launch with four seconds left.
The download keeps *aborting* halfway through.

gloss: To stop doing something, especially when told to.
examples: The letter ordered them to *desist* immediately.
They *desisted* only after the second warning.
He kept calling, *desisting* for a day and then starting again.
contrast: It takes *from*: *desist from further contact*. Americans meet it mostly in the legal phrase *cease and desist*.

gloss: To hold yourself back from doing something.
examples: Please *refrain* from using flash photography.
She *refrained* from saying what she really thought.
He has *refrained* from commenting on the case.
contrast: Always *refrain from doing*, with the -ing form, never *refrain to do*.

gloss: To keep something harmful from growing or spreading.
examples: The city is trying to *curb* speeding near schools.
New rules *curbed* the worst of the spending.
Inflation has been *curbed*, at least for now.

gloss: To cut something short or reduce it before its normal end.
examples: Bad weather may *curtail* the search.
They *curtailed* the tour after three cities.
Services have been *curtailed* because of the budget.

gloss: To stop something from flowing or spreading.
examples: Nothing they tried could *stem* the flood of complaints.
The new coach *stemmed* the losing streak.
They are *stemming* the bleeding with a tourniquet.
contrast: The m doubles: *stemmed*, *stemming*. Note the other sense with *from*: *Her fear stems from an accident years ago.*

gloss: To stop something from being expressed or from developing.
examples: Too many rules can *stifle* new ideas.
She *stifled* a laugh behind her hand.
Debate was *stifled* before it started.

gloss: To put an end to unrest, fear, or doubt.
examples: A short statement should *quell* the rumors.
Police *quelled* the disturbance within an hour.
Her calm voice was *quelling* the panic in the room.

gloss: To stop something firmly, or to cancel a legal decision.
examples: The coach moved fast to *quash* the trade rumors.
The judge *quashed* the subpoena.
The story was *quashed* before it ever ran.

gloss: To put out a fire or a light, or to end something completely.
examples: Please *extinguish* all candles before you leave.
Crews *extinguished* the fire by dawn.
Any hope of a deal had been *extinguished*.

gloss: To get rid of a plan or a thing because it is no longer wanted.
examples: We may have to *scrap* the whole design.
They *scrapped* the fee after a hundred angry emails.
The program is being *scrapped* at the end of the year.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: *scrapped*, *scrapping*.

gloss: To ruin a plan or an agreement so that it cannot go ahead.
examples: One bad headline could *scuttle* the merger.
A single vote *scuttled* the bill.
The deal was *scuttled* at the last minute.

gloss: To reject or cancel something, in informal American English.
examples: My boss will probably *nix* the idea.
The landlord *nixed* our plan for a dog.
The trip was *nixed* because of the storm.

gloss: To officially cancel a decision, order, or offer.
examples: The board can *rescind* the rule at any meeting.
The company *rescinded* the job offer a week later.
The order was quietly *rescinded* in March.

gloss: To declare officially that something has no legal force.
examples: A court can *annul* a marriage in certain cases.
The election results were *annulled*.
They spent a year *annulling* the contract.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: *annulled*, *annulling*.

gloss: To make a document, ticket, or agreement no longer valid.
examples: Opening the case will *void* the warranty.
The clerk *voided* the receipt and rang it up again.
The check had already been *voided*.

gloss: To cancel the effect or the legal force of something.
examples: One missing signature can *nullify* the whole agreement.
The penalty *nullified* the touchdown.
Their gains were *nullified* by rising costs.
contrast: -y after a consonant becomes -ie-: *nullifies*, *nullified* — but *nullifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To make something no longer valid or no longer true.
examples: A late entry will *invalidate* your ticket.
The new data *invalidated* their first conclusion.
Thousands of ballots were *invalidated* over a technicality.

gloss: To cancel out the effect of something.
examples: One late payment can *negate* months of progress.
The extra fees *negated* the savings.
Their advantage was *negated* by the weather.

ru: отклонять, отменять (решение), не принимать во внимание
gloss: To decide against someone's opinion or decision using higher authority.
examples: The judge may *overrule* the objection.
The committee *overruled* her on every point.
We were *overruled* by a single vote.
contrast: Two r's, because it is *over* plus *rule*: *overrule*, *overruled*.

gloss: To refuse to accept or permit something officially.
examples: The referee can *disallow* a goal for offside.
The auditor *disallowed* half the expenses.
Their second claim was *disallowed*.
contrast: Two s's and two l's, because it is *dis* plus *allow*. The respelling LOW here rhymes with *now*, not with *snow*.

gloss: To give up a claim, a belief, or a position publicly.
examples: He had to *renounce* his claim to the property.
She *renounced* violence in her first speech.
They have *renounced* the agreement entirely.

gloss: To give up something you hold, such as control or a right.
examples: He refused to *relinquish* the keys.
She *relinquished* control of the company in 2020.
The title was *relinquished* without a fight.

gloss: To stop someone from doing what they were trying to do.
examples: A locked gate can *thwart* most thieves.
Rain *thwarted* our plans for the whole weekend.
The attack was *thwarted* by an alert guard.

gloss: To prevent a plan, especially a bad one, from succeeding.
examples: A neighbor's dog helped *foil* the break-in.
Her quick thinking *foiled* the scam.
The plot was *foiled* days before it started.

gloss: To make it harder for something to move forward.
examples: Heavy bags will only *hinder* you on the trail.
Fog *hindered* the rescue for hours.
The search was *hindered* by darkness.

gloss: To slow or block the progress of something.
examples: Parked cars *impede* the snowplows.
The injury *impeded* his recovery all season.
Traffic was *impeding* every ambulance downtown.

gloss: To make an activity difficult by getting in its way.
examples: A thick coat can *hamper* your movement.
High winds *hampered* the firefighters.
The investigation has been *hampered* by missing records.

ru: срывать, пускать под откос; сходить с рельсов
transitivity: both — transitive (derail the talks), intransitive (the train derailed)
gloss: To make a plan or a process go badly wrong, or to run off the rails.
examples: One rude question can *derail* the whole interview.
The freight train *derailed* outside town.
The talks were *derailed* by a leaked memo.

gloss: To stop something from happening at all.
examples: A smoke alarm can *prevent* a tragedy.
The rain *prevented* us from finishing the game.
Most of these accidents could have been *prevented*.
contrast: The pattern is *prevent someone from doing something*, with *from* and the -ing form.

gloss: To prevent something bad that was about to happen.
examples: A last-minute deal may *avert* a strike.
Quick thinking *averted* a serious accident.
Disaster was *averted* by a matter of seconds.

gloss: To stop something by acting before it can happen.
examples: They cut prices to *forestall* a walkout.
The apology *forestalled* a much bigger fight.
A lawsuit has been *forestalled*, at least for now.

gloss: To act first so that something else cannot happen or go on.
examples: She tried to *preempt* the question by answering it first.
The network *preempted* the show for a news bulletin.
Our objection had already been *preempted*.
contrast: Also written *pre-empt*; the one-word spelling is the usual American one.

gloss: To try to stop someone from doing something, or to take away their confidence.
examples: High fees *discourage* casual buyers.
Her parents *discouraged* her from moving so far away.
Do not be *discouraged* by the first attempt.
contrast: Like *prevent*, it takes *from* plus -ing: *discouraged him from applying*.

gloss: To stop something on the way and keep it from reaching its destination.
examples: Filters *intercept* most spam before you see it.
A safety *intercepted* the pass in the end zone.
The package was *intercepted* at the border.

gloss: To make something or someone completely unable to move or function.
examples: A storm like that can *paralyze* the whole city.
The strike *paralyzed* shipping for a week.
He was *paralyzed* with stage fright.
contrast: American spelling is *paralyze*; British is *paralyse*.

gloss: To stop something from moving or working.
examples: A splint will *immobilize* the wrist.
The flood *immobilized* half the fleet.
The truck sat *immobilized* in the mud for two days.
contrast: American -ize; British spelling is *immobilise*.

gloss: To damage something so badly that it can barely work.
examples: Another bad season could *cripple* the business.
The outage *crippled* the airline for two days.
Their supply chain has been *crippled* by the shortage.

transitivity: both — transitive (debt hobbles the company), intransitive (he hobbled to the car)
gloss: To hold something back so it can barely move, or to walk with difficulty.
examples: Debt continues to *hobble* the school district.
She *hobbled* off the field on one leg.
The team has been *hobbled* by injuries all year.

gloss: To stop something from growing or developing properly.
examples: Too little light will *stunt* the seedlings.
The drought *stunted* the corn that year.
Their growth has been *stunted* by years of neglect.

transitivity: both — transitive (disband the committee), intransitive (the band disbanded)
gloss: To break up a group so that it stops existing.
examples: The city may *disband* the task force.
The band *disbanded* after their second album.
The unit was *disbanded* in 1995.

ru: отсоединять, разъединять; выходить из контакта, отстраняться
transitivity: both — transitive (disengage the clutch), intransitive (the troops disengaged)
gloss: To stop being connected to or involved in something.
examples: *Disengage* the parking brake before you pull out.
He slowly *disengaged* from the conversation.
The autopilot had *disengaged* without warning.
contrast: When it means to stop taking part, it takes *from*: *disengage from the argument*.

gloss: To close a business or a building down, usually for good.
examples: The chain plans to *shutter* twelve stores.
They *shuttered* the plant in December.
Half the downtown storefronts are *shuttered*.
contrast: Regular, unlike the irregular *shut* (*shut, shut, shut*): *shutter, shuttered, shuttered*.

gloss: To close a business by selling everything it owns.
examples: They will have to *liquidate* the inventory.
The court *liquidated* the firm last spring.
The estate is being *liquidated* to pay the debts.

gloss: To send workers home for a period without pay, usually temporarily.
examples: The airline may *furlough* another thousand workers.
They *furloughed* most of the staff in April.
She was *furloughed* for six weeks and then called back.
contrast: The -gh is silent: FUR-loh, the same ending sound as *though*.

ru: отстранять, выводить из игры, оставлять не у дел
gloss: To keep a person or a project out of the action for a while.
examples: A sprained ankle could *sideline* him for a month.
The flu *sidelined* three of our best players.
She has been *sidelined* since the reorganization.

gloss: To get rid of something completely.
examples: The new system should *eliminate* most of the paperwork.
They *eliminated* forty positions last quarter.
Our team was *eliminated* in the first round.

gloss: To keep something dangerous from spreading any further.
examples: Crews are working to *contain* the fire.
They *contained* the outbreak within two weeks.
The spill has been *contained*, officials said.

gloss: To set an upper limit on an amount so that it stops rising.
examples: The state may *cap* tuition increases.
They *capped* the class at twenty students.
Rent is *capped* at three percent a year.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: *capped*, *capping*.

gloss: To keep something or someone inside limits.
examples: Let us *confine* the discussion to the budget.
The flu *confined* her to bed for a week.
The damage was *confined* to the first floor.
contrast: It takes *to*: *confined to bed*, *confine it to one page*.

gloss: To officially keep someone out or stop them from doing something.
examples: The rule would *bar* anyone under eighteen.
The league *barred* him for a full season.
Reporters were *barred* from the courtroom.
contrast: The r doubles: *barred*, *barring*. It takes *from*: *barred from the building*.

ru: запрещать полёты, оставлять на земле; наказывать (запретом выходить)
gloss: To keep an aircraft on the ground, or to stop a young person from going out.
examples: Fog may *ground* every flight this morning.
My parents *grounded* me for two weeks.
The whole fleet has been *grounded* pending inspection.
contrast: This verb is regular — *ground, grounded, grounded*. Do not confuse it with *ground*, the past tense of the irregular *grind*.

gloss: To make someone or something stop making noise or stop speaking.
examples: Please *silence* your phones before the show.
One look from her *silenced* the whole table.
Critics were being *silenced* one by one.

gloss: To stop resisting and accept what the other side wants.
examples: He refused to *capitulate* on the price.
The company *capitulated* after three weeks of picketing.
They have *capitulated* to almost every demand.
contrast: It takes *to*: *capitulate to pressure*.

gloss: To finally agree after refusing, or to become less severe.
examples: She kept asking until her father *relented*.
The heat shows no sign of *relenting*.
They have *relented* and extended the deadline.

gloss: To leave a place or a position so that it is empty.
examples: Guests must *vacate* the room by eleven.
They *vacated* the apartment in a single afternoon.
The seat was *vacated* when he resigned.

ru: уходить на пенсию, выходить в отставку; выводить из эксплуатации
transitivity: both — transitive (retire the old buses), intransitive (she retired last year)
gloss: To stop working for good, or to take something out of service.
examples: He plans to *retire* at sixty-five.
She *retired* after thirty years at the same school.
The airline is *retiring* its oldest planes.
contrast: With a job it takes *from*: *retired from teaching*.

transitivity: both — transitive (taper the dose), intransitive (the rain tapered)
gloss: To become gradually smaller or less, or to reduce something gradually.
examples: The doctor will *taper* the medication over a month.
The applause *tapered* into silence.
Demand has been *tapering* since July.
contrast: The r is not doubled, because the stress is on the first syllable: *tapered*, *tapering*.

gloss: To continue for a period of time, or to remain usable.
examples: The meeting should *last* about an hour.
The storm *lasted* well into the night.
These boots have *lasted* me nine winters.
contrast: In American English the vowel is /æ/, the same as in *ask* and *class*.

gloss: To continue to exist, or to keep doing something despite difficulty.
examples: If the pain *persists*, call your doctor.
She *persisted* until somebody finally listened.
The rumors have *persisted* for years.
contrast: For an action it takes *in* plus -ing: *persisted in asking*.

ru: упорствовать, не сдаваться, продолжать несмотря ни на что
gloss: To keep going at something difficult without giving up.
examples: You have to *persevere* through the boring part.
They *persevered* for three seasons before winning anything.
She has *persevered* despite every setback.
contrast: It takes *with* or *in*: *persevere with the training*. Do not confuse it with *preserve* (to keep something from spoiling) — a different verb entirely.

gloss: To continue to be the case, or to win in the end.
examples: Common sense usually *prevails* in the end.
Their side *prevailed* by two votes.
The *prevailing* winds come from the west.
contrast: To beat someone it takes *over* or *against*: *prevailed over a stronger team*.

ru: задерживаться, медлить; сохраняться, долго не проходить
gloss: To stay longer than expected, or to be slow to disappear.
examples: A few guests always *linger* after the party.
The smell of smoke *lingered* for days.
She has been *lingering* by the door for ten minutes.

gloss: To continue longer than something or someone else.
examples: This coat will *outlast* three cheap ones.
Their patience *outlasted* ours.
The old bridge has *outlasted* every engineer who doubted it.

gloss: To live or remain useful longer than someone or something else.
examples: She *outlived* her husband by twenty years.
That joke has *outlived* its usefulness.
Few buildings *outlive* their architects.

gloss: To make something continue, especially something that should stop.
examples: These ads only *perpetuate* the stereotype.
The policy *perpetuated* the same gap for decades.
The myth is *perpetuated* every time somebody repeats it.

gloss: To happen again, especially more than once.
examples: The problem *recurs* every time it rains.
The pain *recurred* two months later.
It is a *recurring* charge, not a one-time fee.
contrast: Stress is on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *recurred*, *recurring*.

gloss: To say something again for emphasis or clarity.
examples: Let me *reiterate* that nobody is losing their job.
She *reiterated* the offer in writing.
The mayor has *reiterated* his support twice this week.

gloss: To stay where you are or delay acting until something happens.
examples: Can you *wait* five more minutes?
We *waited* almost an hour for a table.
She has been *waiting* outside since noon.
contrast: It takes *for* before a person or thing and *to* before a verb: *wait for the bus*, *wait to hear back*. It sounds exactly like *weight*.

transitivity: both — transitive (rest your eyes), intransitive (rest for an hour)
gloss: To stop activity for a while in order to recover.
examples: You should *rest* that knee for a few days.
We *rested* at the top of the hill.
He has been *resting* since the surgery.

gloss: To put something off until a later time.
examples: You can *defer* the payment for ninety days.
They *deferred* the decision until after the holidays.
Her admission was *deferred* to the spring semester.
contrast: Stress is on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *deferred*, *deferring*. With *to* it means something else — to yield to someone: *I defer to her judgment.*

ru: откладывать на потом, тянуть время, медлить
gloss: To keep putting off something you should be doing.
examples: I always *procrastinate* when the job is boring.
He *procrastinated* until the night before it was due.
Stop *procrastinating* and send the email.

gloss: To postpone discussion of a proposal until later.
examples: Let us *table* that question for now.
The council *tabled* the motion until June.
The proposal was *tabled* and never came back.
contrast: A true US/UK trap: in American English *table a proposal* means to set it aside, while in British English it means to bring it forward for discussion.

gloss: To stop using something and store it in case it is needed later.
examples: They may *mothball* the second factory.
The Navy *mothballed* four ships that year.
The project has been *mothballed* since the funding dried up.

gloss: To pause an official meeting or session for a period.
examples: The court will *recess* until two o'clock.
Congress *recessed* for the holidays.
The hearing has *recessed* twice already today.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, rih-SES; the noun (school recess) is stressed on the first: REE-ses.

gloss: To move or act more slowly than you should.
examples: Do not *dawdle* — the bus leaves at eight.
The kids *dawdled* all the way home.
She was *dawdling* over her cereal again.

gloss: To lose strength or momentum and nearly stop.
examples: Sales began to *falter* in the second quarter.
His voice *faltered* halfway through the speech.
The recovery is *faltering* again.

gloss: To hesitate between choices, or to become unsteady.
examples: She never *wavered* in her decision.
Support for the plan is *wavering*.
He *wavers* every time the price goes up.
contrast: Do not confuse it with the noun *waiver* (a signed form giving up a right); the two sound alike but are spelled differently.

ru: истекать (о сроке), прекращать действие; впадать (в состояние)
gloss: To come to an end because it was not renewed, or to slip into a state.
examples: Your membership will *lapse* on the first.
The insurance *lapsed* while he was overseas.
The room had *lapsed* into silence.
contrast: *Lapse* is about a right or a policy ending; *elapse* is about time passing. A permit lapses; three hours elapse.

gloss: To pass, said of a period of time.
examples: Six months must *elapse* before you can reapply.
Two hours had *elapsed* before anyone noticed.
The *elapsed* time is shown at the bottom of the screen.
contrast: Only time elapses. People and things do not elapse — compare *lapse*, which is what an unrenewed license does.

gloss: To become less intense and gradually stop.
examples: The swelling should *subside* in a day or two.
The noise *subsided* once the band left.
The floodwater has finally *subsided*.

gloss: To become less strong or less severe.
examples: The wind should *abate* by evening.
Demand *abated* after the holidays.
The storm showed no sign of *abating*.

gloss: To get gradually smaller, weaker, or less important.
examples: Interest in the show began to *wane*.
His influence *waned* after the election.
The moon is *waning* this week.

gloss: To flow back or gradually decrease.
examples: The tide begins to *ebb* around four.
Her strength *ebbed* through the long night.
Support for the measure has been *ebbing* for months.

gloss: To move back or become more distant, and so fade away.
examples: The water should *recede* by morning.
The danger *receded* as quickly as it came.
His hairline has been *receding* since college.

gloss: To complete something that was promised or required.
examples: You must *fulfill* the residency requirement first.
They *fulfilled* every order before Christmas.
The contract has not been *fulfilled*.
contrast: American spelling doubles the final l: *fulfill*, *fulfills*. British English writes *fulfil*, *fulfils* — but both sides write *fulfilled* and *fulfilling*.

gloss: To reach the final and highest point of a process.
examples: The festival *culminates* in a parade downtown.
Years of work *culminated* in a single afternoon.
The tour is *culminating* with two nights in Chicago.
contrast: It takes *in* or *with*, never a direct object: *culminated in a lawsuit*.

gloss: To settle something finally, especially a deal or a victory.
examples: One more win will *clinch* the division.
Her last answer *clinched* the interview.
The deal was *clinched* over dinner.

gloss: To finish a course of study and receive a diploma or degree.
examples: She will *graduate* in May.
He *graduated* from Ohio State in 2016.
Only half the class is *graduating* on time.
contrast: Americans say *graduate from* a school. The verb ends in -ayt; the noun *a graduate* ends in -uht: GRAJ-oo-uht.

gloss: To get involved where you are not wanted, or to get in the way of something.
examples: Try not to *interfere* with their routine.
The noise *interfered* with the recording.
She has been *interfering* in her son's marriage for years.
contrast: *Interfere with* something (an activity, a signal), but *interfere in* something (someone's private business).

transitivity: both — transitive (interject a question), intransitive (may I interject?)
gloss: To say something suddenly in the middle of someone else's speech.
examples: May I *interject* for one second?
He *interjected* a question halfway through.
She kept *interjecting* until the chair cut her off.

gloss: To take someone's attention away from what they are doing.
examples: Loud music *distracts* me when I am working.
The dog *distracted* him at exactly the wrong moment.
I was *distracted* by a text and missed the turn.
contrast: It takes *from*: *distracted him from his homework*.
